# **Lane T3b: What Grew Where on Pre-Eruption Thera, and How Thickly (Late May, 1615 BCE)**

In late May 1615 BCE on the high radiocarbon chronology (roughly 0–15 years before the Late Bronze Age eruption on classic late-17th-century models, or \~45–70 years before it on mid-16th-century radiocarbon revisions), Thera was neither bare white pumice nor closed forest, but an intensively used volcanic-and-limestone island combining arable lowlands, managed olive groves, open oak-and-pine woodland, grazed scrub, and bare rock cliffs1. Direct Grade A constraints come from Akrotiri's wood charcoal and crop assemblages, buried rural sites, in-situ tree remains, and pre-eruption bedrock geology, while planting densities, canopy covers, shrub heights, and Munsell soil colours must be parameterized from contemporary Bronze Age Aegean parallels (Grade B) and later/modern Mediterranean benchmarks (Grade C), with post-eruption white pumice (*aspa*) and modern *kouloura* basket-trained vines strictly excluded from baseline assumptions2. Direct Munsell colours for Thera's buried Minoan palaeosol, pre-eruption agricultural terrace walls on Thera itself, island-wide biome area shares, and direct dung or manuring-isotope analyses from Late Cycladic I Thera could not be verified in accessible sources and are flagged plainly below.

## **1\. Summary**

* **Strip out modern Santorini's white pumice blanket first:** The up to 60 m mantle of white/light-grey Minoan tephra (Munsell 5Y 7/1) and sandy *aspa* soil postdates 1615 BCE; pre-eruption Thera exposed dark northern lavas, red Cape Riva ignimbrite (21.8–22 ka), rust-red Akrotiri scoria cones, grey-brown older tuffs, and southeastern crystalline limestone and green phyllite-schist, topped by a thin, eroded palaeosol (0.5 m in the Fira reference section, locally 3–4 m) (**Claims 13a–14d, 42a–44d, 48c–48d**)4.  
* **Model an open agricultural-and-woodland mosaic, not closed forest:** Late Cycladic I charcoal from Akrotiri shaft 63A is dominated by olive prunings (68.0%), alongside pine (7.0%, down from 36.4% in EBA), cypress/juniper (7.0%), deciduous oak (5.5%), evergreen oak (3.9%), and maquis/garigue/garden shrubs (*Arbutus*, *Punica*, *Lonicera*, *Fabaceae*, plus EBA–MBA *Rhamnus*, *Capparis*, *Lamiaceae*), indicating managed groves, open woodland, and grazed scrub (**Claims 19–21b, 23**)2.  
* **Exclude imported timbers and Pleistocene fossil palms from 1615 BCE flora:** Cedar (*Cedrus libani*), yew (*Taxus baccata*), and beech (*Fagus*) in Akrotiri charcoal were overseas imports, while in-situ dwarf fan palms (*Chamaerops humilis*, 2–3 m tall) and fossil palm/olive leaves in Fira tuffs date to \~37,000–60,000 yr BP (Late Pleistocene), not the Bronze Age (**Claims 17a–17b, 22**)2.  
* **Do not spawn fresco-only plants or permanent rivers as terrain defaults:** Saffron crocus (which blooms exclusively in autumn, so dormant in late May), hybrid red/white lilies, papyrus, palms, and myrtle appear in Akrotiri wall paintings without verified Bronze Age macroremains on Thera, whereas reeds, pine, and fig are both painted and physically attested; pre-eruption Thera had no permanent rivers, only seasonal winter/spring torrent beds and limestone cave springs on Profitis Ilias (566 m) (**Claims 24a–24d, 28a–29**)2.  
* **Place intensive farmland and rural villas across the gentler Akrotiri Peninsula hinterland:** Dense \~20 ha urban Akrotiri lacked private gardens and received grain already cleaned of chaff (with only one wine press found in \~1 ha), while outlying LBA sites—including the walled-courtyard villa at Raos (\<1 km NW), the chaff-and-livestock complex at Balos (62 m a.s.l.), Ftellos (house with circular pen), Potamos-Kamaras, Chalarovounia, and Alaphouzos (Therasia)—occupied the arable and pastoral countryside (**Claims 1–6c**)5.  
* **Treat pre-eruption farm terraces on Thera as unverified locally, though plausible on \>10°–12° tilled slopes:** The burnt terraced stones with a charred olive shrub under pumice at Koimisis (Therasia) belong to a ruined EBA–MC settlement abandoned before LC I, and caldera-wall concentric ledges are interpreted as natural erosional benches; however, contemporary Bronze Age agricultural terraces and check-dams are documented on Kythera and Crete (Pseira, Choiromandres) (**Claims 7a–12b**)1.  
* **Use late-May phenology for crops, orchards, and scrub:** In late May, pulses (*Lathyrus clymenum*, pea, lentil) are being harvested or freshly cut, autumn-sown barley is ripening golden ahead of June cereal harvest, olives are inside their April–June Mediterranean flowering window, grapevines are in active spring bud differentiation (May 15–June 15), and Mediterranean phrygana shrubs are shifting to summer leaves (**Claims 26a–26f, 33a–33b, 35b, 37a–37b, 38f**)31.  
* **Parameterize dry-farmed olive groves at sparse ancient/traditional spacing (Grade C):** Use \~60 trees/ha (polycropped with wheat) to 100 trees/ha (monoculture, 10 m spacing) for ancient Greek models, or 40–250 trees/ha (typical dry Mediterranean 100–200 trees/ha at 5–7 × 6–8 m) with pruned, open-centred canopies \~3–6 m tall (**Claims 31–32c**)8.  
* **Do not assume modern *kouloura* basket vines for 1615 BCE (Grade C):** Santorini's low basket-trained vines (10–20 cm tall, 1,800–2,200 vines/ha) adapted to post-eruption pumice and extreme drought; prehistoric Aegean vines could be grown as low bushes, ground-sprawling, trellised/staked, or climbing trees (rainfed Mediterranean wide-row benchmarks: 2,500–3,333 vines/ha at 3–4 m rows) (**Claims 34a–35a**)7.  
* **Scatter open woodland and grazed scrub by slope and exposure (Grades A & C):** Place open oak woodland (50–60 trees/ha Greek average, 40–50% canopy cover; Cycladic Kea 160 trees/ha at 3–10 m height) and open *Pinus halepensis/brutia* stands (100–250 trees/ha, 11–40% cover) in sheltered gullies, north slopes, and Profitis Ilias limestone; cover steep grazed volcanic slopes with phrygana (\<50 cm tall, \~30% or \>30% dwarf woody cover, \<15% sclerophyll canopy) grading into maquis (1–3 m tall, 15–47% cover) (**Claims 20, 25, 27a–27b, 38a–41e**)2.  
* **Anchor shoreline and dry torrent strips with tamarisk, reeds, pebbles, and beachrock:** Along Akrotiri's indented pre-eruption south-coast coves and seasonal torrent outflows (such as Potamos Kamaras), place brackish/coastal *Tamarix*, *Phragmites australis* reed stands, sea-pebble shores, and beachrock slabs (**Claims 24a–24d, 45a–45b**)2.  
* **Use comparative Munsell palettes with explicit Grade C flags:** Because direct Munsell measurements of Thera's buried Minoan palaeosol, schist soils, and pre-eruption beach sand could not be verified, parameterize bare soil on Profitis Ilias limestone as terra rossa (5YR 3/3 to 2.5YR 3/4–5/8), hillslope soils as reddish-brown to brown Cambisols (5YR 4/4–3/4, 7.5YR 4/3), and weathered older volcanic tuff soils as dark brown to dark yellowish-brown (7.5YR–10YR; moist 10YR 3/3–4/4) (**Claims 46–48b**)52.

## **4\. Assumptions checked**

* **T3b-1:** Could not verify directly on Thera or Therasia — Koimisis burnt terraced stones with a charred olive shrub belong to a ruined EBA–MC habitation site abandoned before LC I (**Claims 7a–8b**), caldera-wall concentric ledges are interpreted as natural erosional benches (**Claim 9**), and no excavated pre-eruption farm terrace on Thera is verified (**Claims 10a–10b**), though contemporary Bronze Age farm terraces exist on Kythera and Crete (**Claims 11a–12b**)1.  
* **T3b-2:** Partly confirmed — a buried palaeosol lies directly beneath the Minoan tephra across Thera and Therasia (**Claims 13a–14d**), and isolated in-situ finds (Phira olive tree, Koimisis olive shrub, Athinios tree cavities, buried roots) anchor point locations (**Claims 7a, 15a–16c**), but remains are too sparse to map island-wide zones directly and older \~37–60 ka Pleistocene floras must be kept separate (**Claims 17a–17b**)1.  
* **T3b-3:** Partly confirmed — extensive arable ground on the Akrotiri Peninsula, outlying processing and residential sites (Raos, Balos, Ftellos), clean urban grain at Akrotiri, rich olive/cereal/pulse assemblages, and caprine husbandry support farmed gentler lowlands and grazed steep/rocky slopes (**Claims 1–6c, 19, 26a–27b**), but exact field boundaries and land-use area shares under the pumice remain unverified (**Claim 30**)5.  
* **T3b-4:** Confirmed — Akrotiri wood charcoal blends dominant managed olive (68.0% LBA) with declining pine, cypress/juniper, deciduous and evergreen oak, and light-demanding maquis/garigue shrubs alongside scarce LC I structural pine, indicating open woodland, groves, and scrub rather than closed forest (**Claims 19–21b, 23, 40a–41e**)2.  
* **T3b-5:** Partly confirmed — no pre-eruption subfossil pollen record from Thera itself was found in surveyed Aegean palynological syntheses (only a modern Akrotiri vineyard surface sample is reported, and dry southern Aegean strata preserve pollen poorly), though unpublished negative tests cannot be ruled out (**Claims 18a–18b**)69.  
* **T3b-6:** Confirmed — no Bronze Age archaeological or iconographic evidence confirms Santorini's modern basket-trained *kouloura* vines for 1615 BCE; *kouloura* adapted to post-eruption pumice and extreme drought, whereas prehistoric Aegean vines could be grown as low bushes, ground-sprawling, trellised/staked, or tree-climbing (**Claims 34a–34e, 42a–42b**)7.

## **5\. Debates**

**Eruption date and distance from 1615 BCE.** Friedrich et al. (2006) wiggle-matched 72 X-ray CT rings in the Phira Quarry olive branch to 1627–1600 BCE (95% IntCal04)65, and Manning (2022; 2024 Bayesian peak \~1608 BCE, 2σ 1618–1584 BCE) maintains a late-17th to very early-16th-century BCE eruption3. Conversely, Cherubini et al. (2014) challenged olive ring counting (44% average deviation across ten experts on modern Santorini olive wood)92, and Ehrlich et al. (2021) plus Raj et al. (2023) showed that masked growth rings (nearly 30 years hidden in a modern outer 1.5 cm radius), localized growth cessation (\~20 yr), circumferential age offsets (\~40 yr), and moving-average block calibration shift the Phira branch into the mid-16th century BCE31. Pearson et al. (2023) reinforced a mid-16th-century shift via the younger Therasia olive shoot (1602–1502 BCE at 95.4% IntCal20)1, while Egyptian-linked chronologies place the eruption c. 1540–1500 BCE1. For world-building, 1615 BCE sits \~0–15 years before the eruption under classic high models, or \~45–70 years before it (near the late MC/early LC I earthquake repair horizon) under mid-16th-century radiocarbon models.  
**Moist open woodland versus drier thermophilous scrub and poor soils.** Asouti (2003) read Akrotiri's deciduous/evergreen oaks, pine, cypress/juniper, and troglodytic leaf-litter beetle as evidence for a relatively moist, cool Bronze Age climate supporting open oak woodland2. By contrast, Mavromati (2017, 2021\) emphasizes continuous thermophilous Mediterranean vegetation from Early Cycladic to LC I and notes that pine (*Pinus* tp. *brutia/halepensis*) had grown scarce enough by LC I to push builders into emergency earthquake repairs using olive, tamarisk, and fig15; Davidson (1978) likewise concluded that pre-eruption Minoan soils were poorly developed, eroded, and fertility-limited4.  
**Arable cropping regime: bare fallow, cereal–pulse rotation, or maslin.** Classical Greek agronomic models (Foxhall 2007\) assume biennial bare fallow (\~50% cropped, \~50% fallow each year) to conserve water and soil nutrients9. Archaeobotanists led by Sarpaki (1992) and Halstead argue that intensive legume cultivation—exemplified by pure stored crops of drought-tolerant *Lathyrus clymenum* at Akrotiri—supported nitrogen-fixing cereal–pulse rotation that reduced bare fallow74, whereas Sallares (1991) suggests cereals and legumes were grown simultaneously in mixed fields (maslins)75.  
**Wild versus cultivated crocus and realism in Theran wall paintings.** Sarpaki (2000), Amigues, and Porter identify the Xeste 3 crocuses as wild *Crocus cartwrightianus* gathered on rocky phrygana hills, whereas Morgan (1988) and Rackham favoured cultivated *C. sativus* or garden contexts18. More broadly, Day (2011, 2013\) cautions that Akrotiri's floral wall paintings blend traits of different species (such as white *Lilium candidum* and red *L. chalcedonicum*) and depict flora unverified in local Bronze Age macroremains, making them unreliable as direct vegetation maps18.  
**Age of Santorini's *kouloura* vine training.** Contemporary viticultural literature describes *kouloura* as practised "for centuries" or "thousands of years" on Santorini's volcanic ground10, whereas Sarpaki (2012) emphasizes that prehistoric Aegean viticulture used diverse training forms (ground, bush, trellis, tree-climbing) and no Bronze Age physical or iconographic evidence confirms *kouloura* before the post-eruption pumice landscape7.

## **6\. Game hooks**

*All paragraphs below are **design suggestions** (Grade C / INFERENCE), kept separate from the sourced evidence tables to support procedural code implementation.*  
**Suggestion — Terrain-Driven Procedural Biome Shader and Scatter Ruleset.** Drive ground shaders and procedural plant instancing from four continuous map channels: **slope angle**, **pre-eruption bedrock lithology**, **aspect (north vs. south)**, and **distance from Akrotiri and outlying estates**. On the gentler volcanic slopes of the Akrotiri Peninsula (\<10°–12°), apply dark brown to reddish-brown Cambisol/tuff soil shaders (Munsell 7.5YR 4/3 to 10YR 3/3–4/4) divided into irregular small plots that showcase late-May harvest contrast: freshly cut pale stubble on early-harvested pulse plots (*Lathyrus clymenum*, pea, lentil), golden ripening barley ready for June sickles, greener-gold wheat, and ploughed or weed-flecked fallow32. Scatter dry-farmed olive groves at 60 trees/ha (polycropped with grain) up to 100–150 trees/ha (monoculture groves), using low open-centred canopies 3–5 m tall dusted with pale cream-yellow late-May olive blossoms9.  
**Suggestion — Outskirts, Vineyards, and Steep Volcanic Slopes.** Keep dense \~20 ha Akrotiri tight and courtyard-free with flat roof-working decks, while placing rural agricultural infrastructure outside town around Raos, Balos, Ftellos, and Chalarovounia: robust stone enclosure walls, spacious courtyards, circular stone caprine pens, chaff-strewn clearing areas, and fieldside grape-treading vats5. Render vineyards on sun-exposed lower and mid slopes as low head-trained bush vines (\~0.5–0.8 m tall with fresh green May shoots in bud differentiation) or low reed-staked rows (\~2,000–2,800 vines/ha) rather than ground-coiled modern *kouloura* baskets7. Above 12°–20° on volcanic ridges and caldera cliffs, expose dark andesitic-basaltic lavas, red Cape Riva ignimbrite ledges, and rust-red Mavrorachidi/Red Beach scoria, scattered with grazed phrygana cushions (\<50 cm tall, 30–40% dwarf woody cover shifting from spring green to grey-green summer leaves), goat-browsed maquis (1–2.5 m *Quercus coccifera*, *Pistacia*, *Arbutus*, *Juniperus* at 15–35% cover), and occasional lone hardy olives referencing the Phira rim tree and Koimisis ruins shrub1.  
**Suggestion — Limestone Highlands, Dry Torrents, and Coastline.** On Profitis Ilias (566 m), Mesa Vouno, north-facing slopes, and sheltered ravines, switch bedrock shaders to pale crystalline limestone and greenish-grey Athinios phyllite-schist pocketed with deep red terra rossa (Munsell 5YR 3/3 to 2.5YR 3/4)6. Populate these moister refugia with open deciduous and evergreen oak woodland (50–120 trees/ha, 3–10 m tall, \~40–45% canopy cover) mixed with scattered open *Pinus halepensis/brutia* and cypress stands (80–200 trees/ha, 20–35% cover) thinning toward bare summit karst2. Along the south coast, carve dry, cobble-lined seasonal torrent beds (such as Potamos Kamaras—zero flowing rivers in late May\!) bordered by feathery *Tamarix* shrubs and green *Phragmites* reed clusters near brackish coastal seeps and limestone cave springs, meeting indented pebble-and-beachrock coves2.  
![][image3]  
**Suggestion — Interactive Evidence Lens and Soundscape Hooks.** Add a browser UI toggle allowing users to switch between three views: (1) **1615 BCE Strict Evidence View** (no *kouloura*, no autumn crocus blooms, no unattested palms/papyrus, no flowing rivers); (2) **Fresco-Inspired Overlay** (ghosted botanical markers noting where wall paintings depict autumn crocuses, hybrid lilies, palms, and river scenes without verified local macroremains); and (3) **Modern Santorini Contrast** (draping the light-grey 5Y 7/1 Minoan pumice blanket across the terrain so visitors immediately grasp why modern treeless *aspa* Santorini misleads). Tie procedural ambient audio directly to the biome masks—dry late-May wind rustling golden barley and coastal *Phragmites* reeds, insect hum inside olive groves, and goat clatter on steep phrygana slopes around Balos and Ftellos, while omitting rushing river sound everywhere outside Profitis Ilias cave springs17.
